title: The Jackdaw and the Pigeons
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Jackdaw, watching some Pigeons in a farmyard, was filled with envy when he saw how well they were fed, and determined to disguise himself as one of them, in order to secure a share of the good things they enjoyed. So he painted himself white from head to foot and joined the flock; and, so long as he was silent, they never suspected that he was not a pigeon like themselves.

But one day he was unwise enough to start chattering, when they at once saw through his disguise and pecked him so unmercifully that he was glad to escape and join his own kind again. But the other jackdaws did not recognise him in his white dress, and would not let him feed with them, but drove him away: and so he became a homeless wanderer for his pains.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Jackdaw envy the Pigeons?
options: Because they can fly faster than he can
Because they have prettier feathers than his own
Because he sees how well they are fed
Because they live in a safer part of the farmyard

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Jackdaw disguise himself?
options: He paints himself white from head to foot
He plucks out his own dark feathers
He borrows feathers from a real pigeon
He covers himself in flour from the farmyard

questions.prompt: According to the passage, as long as what does he do, the Pigeons never suspect him?
options: As long as he stays near the edge of the flock
As long as he eats slowly like they do
As long as he only comes out at night
As long as he remains silent

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what mistake does the Jackdaw make one day?
options: He tries to eat too much food at once
He starts chattering
He flies in a way no pigeon would
He falls asleep in full view of the flock

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the Pigeons do once they see through his disguise?
options: They quietly ask him to leave the farmyard
They report him to the farmer at once
They peck him so unmercifully that he is glad to escape
They simply ignore him from then on

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens when the Jackdaw tries to rejoin his own kind?
options: The other jackdaws do not recognise him and drive him away
The other jackdaws welcome him back happily
The other jackdaws laugh at his failed disguise
The other jackdaws ask him to teach them the trick

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does staying silent allow the Jackdaw's disguise to succeed at first?
options: The Pigeons could not see him clearly enough to notice any difference
Silence was a rule all pigeons followed strictly
The Pigeons were too distracted by food to notice him at all
His appearance alone was convincing, but his voice would have given him away

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Jackdaw end up worse off than before his disguise?
options: He is physically unable to fly after being painted white
He loses acceptance from both the Pigeons and his own kind
He is punished by the farmer for stealing food
He forgets how to behave like a jackdaw at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "unmercifully" mean in "pecked him so unmercifully"?
options: Gently, with some hesitation
Quietly, without being noticed
Harshly, without any restraint
Occasionally, now and then

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Trying to pass yourself off as something you are not can leave you belonging nowhere at all
Pigeons are more observant than most other birds
Disguises always work as long as they are convincing enough
Jackdaws and pigeons cannot ever get along together

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does the Jackdaw first observe the Pigeons?
options: In a city square
In an open field
Near a riverbank
In a farmyard

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Jackdaw hope to secure by disguising himself?
options: A safe place to build his nest
A share of the good things the Pigeons enjoyed
Protection from other jackdaws
A chance to learn how pigeons fly

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what color does the Jackdaw paint himself?
options: Gray
Brown
White
Black and white spotted

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why do his fellow jackdaws refuse to accept him back?
options: His white disguise makes him unrecognizable as one of their own
They had already found a replacement for him
They believe he betrayed them by joining the pigeons
They are afraid the Pigeons will attack them too

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "for his pains" suggest about the outcome of his scheme?
options: His efforts were ultimately rewarded despite some difficulty
His pains were physical injuries from the Pigeons' pecking alone
His pains were quickly forgotten once he found a new flock
His efforts to gain something led only to suffering and loss

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "envy" mean in "was filled with envy"?
options: A feeling of deep affection for another
A feeling of wanting what someone else has
A feeling of confusion or uncertainty
A feeling of pride in one's own abilities

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Jackdaw successfully lives among the Pigeons for the rest of his life
A Jackdaw teaches the Pigeons how to disguise themselves too
A Jackdaw disguises himself as a Pigeon, is exposed and rejected, and is then rejected by his own kind as well
A Jackdaw is welcomed back warmly by both groups of birds
